newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak securities law obscure, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Slovak securities law obscure, analysts say.

text.p: The Slovak parliament on Wednesday approved an amendment to the securities law which analysts said will further cloud opaque trading by effectively reinstating dealing outside organised markets.
Analysts and opposition deputies also criticised the amendment for withdrawing the obligation to register stakes in a company.
But legislators rejected a controversial proposal which would have increased the power of majority shareholders.

The amendment, approved by 63 votes to 51 with four abstentions in the 150-seat chamber, reversed an amendment approved last year stipulating that all transactions must be registered at the Central Securities Registry and performed through brokers on organised markets.
Analysts said the new law effectively allows over- the-counter trading without registration on the main markets.

"The amendments in fact bypass the issue (of shareholders' rights) and will considerably damage the transparency of the market," said economist Viliam Vaskovic, a deputy of the opposition Democratic Union.

"If the law in fact allows trading shares outside the scrutiny of the market it could lead to sales to completely unknown buyers, for example even to the Russian mafia," said Martin Barto, an analyst at ING Barings.
Most analysts agreed, however, that this would affect mainly smaller companies and not leading stocks.
Many deals on the Slovak securities market are surrounded by confusion with various authorities and market players issuing often contradictory information.
The government's preferred method of privatisation by direct sale - often through management buyouts - has also raised concern, notably from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Securities dealers also said they feared that the amendment could effectively enable a majority shareholder to cancel trading in an issue on the market.

"Despite rejecting the explicit right of majority shareholders to suspend trading, the amended law has dropped the stipulation forbidding such a move," said Dusan Lachkovic, President of the Slovak Association of Investment Companies. "If something is not forbidden by law, then it is allowed."
"I'm afraid that this is the most ominous paragraph of all," Barto added.
The Securities Act, originally amended last year, sets out ground rules for issuing and trading shares and bonds on Slovak capital markets.
Brokers said last year's law needed a thorough overhaul as, among other things, it did little to protect small shareholders and was incompatible with other related legislation.
